summary: The evidence is inconclusive on whether blue light glasses significantly improve sleep quality for most users. Some controlled studies report modest benefits in sleep onset and self-reported quality, while others show minimal objective differences versus placebo lenses. Effects appear highly context-dependent based on evening screen exposure, lens quality, and baseline sleep habits.

sources.title: Blue-blocking glasses as a treatment for insomnia
sources.quote: Participants in the amber-lens condition reported improved sleep and mood compared with clear-lens controls.
sources.credibility_reason: Peer-reviewed randomized crossover design with direct sleep-related outcomes.

sources.title: Do blue-blocking lenses improve sleep? A systematic review
sources.quote: Evidence was mixed and generally low-certainty due to heterogeneity and small sample sizes.
sources.credibility_reason: Systematic review explicitly grading evidence quality and limitations.

sources.title: American Academy of Ophthalmology guidance
sources.quote: There is not enough evidence to support special blue-blocking eyewear for digital eye strain or sleep in all users.
sources.credibility_reason: Leading professional medical association with conservative evidence standards.

sources.title: Blue-blocking lenses and evening melatonin outcomes
sources.quote: Blue-blocking interventions altered melatonin profiles, but downstream sleep metrics varied considerably across participants.
sources.credibility_reason: Peer-reviewed trial with objective biomarker measurement and transparent caveats.

sources.title: Sleep Foundation evidence summary
sources.quote: Some people may benefit, but more high-quality studies are needed before strong conclusions can be made.
sources.credibility_reason: Evidence review source summarizing peer-reviewed findings with balanced framing.
